description: Checks general classroom practice for pre-primary, primary and secondary teachers: methods, engagement, assessment, inclusion and professional conduct.

competencies.name: Subject knowledge and teaching methods
competencies.description: Understands clear objectives and effective teaching methods such as scaffolding.

competencies.name: Lesson delivery and learner engagement
competencies.description: Keeps learners active, thinking and on task during lessons.

competencies.name: Assessment and feedback
competencies.description: Uses assessment and feedback to guide teaching and help learners improve.

competencies.name: Inclusion and meeting individual needs
competencies.description: Adapts teaching so learners of different abilities and needs can learn.

competencies.name: Child protection and professional conduct
competencies.description: Protects learners from harm and behaves professionally with pupils.

questions.text: Which question is best for making pupils think and explain their ideas in a science lesson?

options.text: "Is the plant leaning towards the window?"
"Why do you think the plant leaned towards the window?"
"What is the name of this plant?"
"Does the plant need light, yes or no?"

questions.explanation: Open 'why' questions make learners reason and explain, while yes/no and naming questions need only short recall.

questions.text: Which is the best-written learning objective for a lesson on flowers?

options.text: The teacher will cover page 24 of the textbook.
Pupils will enjoy the lesson on flowers today.
To teach pupils about the different kinds of flowers that grow in our villages and gardens.
By the end, pupils will be able to name and describe three parts of a flower.

questions.explanation: A good objective says what learners will be able to do, in a way that can be observed and checked.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of formative assessment?

options.text: To give marks that will be printed on the school report at the end of term
To check what learners understand so the teacher can adjust teaching
To rank pupils from first to last in each class at the end of the year
To decide which pupils will be promoted to the next class in January

questions.explanation: Formative assessment happens during learning and is used to improve teaching and learning, not only to give grades.

questions.text: What does 'scaffolding' mean in teaching?

options.text: Giving learners the final answers so they can copy them
Leaving learners to work alone so they learn from mistakes
Giving learners temporary support that is reduced as they become able to work alone
Making all tasks easier for weak learners for the whole year so that they never feel failure

questions.explanation: Scaffolding is support that helps a learner reach a task they cannot yet do alone, then is gradually removed.

questions.text: Which behaviour shows good professional conduct towards pupils?

options.text: Asking older pupils to run personal errands for you after school
Keeping relationships respectful and open, and avoiding private meetings behind closed doors
Accepting friend requests from pupils on personal social media so you can keep in touch about homework
Giving small gifts to favourite pupils who get high marks

questions.explanation: Professional teachers keep clear boundaries and transparent relationships that protect both pupils and themselves.

questions.text: Which actions help include learners with different abilities in one class? Select all that apply.

options.text: Explaining ideas with objects and pictures as well as words
Using one method only, copying notes from the board
Giving challenging questions only to the strongest learners
Giving tasks at different levels of difficulty on the same topic
Seating slower learners at the back so they do not disturb others

questions.explanation: Different task levels and several ways of explaining let more learners understand and take part.

questions.text: Which activities are learner-centred? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pupils prepare a short demonstration of a method for classmates
Small groups build a model and explain it to the class
Pupils silently copy notes from the board for the whole period
Pairs discuss a problem and then share their answers (think-pair-share)
The teacher answers every question and pupils only listen

questions.explanation: Learner-centred activities make pupils discuss, make and explain, not only listen or copy.

questions.text: Which exam question best tests higher-order thinking (judging and justifying)?

options.text: "Two farmers store maize differently. Which way suits your village better, and why?"
"List three ways of storing maize after harvest and write them neatly in your book."
"Define the word 'storage' in your own words and give one example from your home."
"Copy the diagram of a maize granary into your book and label all of its main parts."

questions.explanation: Comparing options and giving reasons requires evaluation, while listing, defining and copying require only recall.

questions.text: Five pupils finish the class exercise much earlier than the others and begin to disturb their neighbours. What is the best response?

options.text: Let them leave the room quietly and wait outside under a tree until the rest of the class finishes
Give them the same exercise again to repeat
Give them an extension task that deepens the same topic, such as making their own problem
Tell them to sit with folded arms until others finish

questions.explanation: Extension tasks keep fast learners thinking and on topic, which also reduces disturbance.

questions.text: After a short quiz, 18 of your 40 pupils give the same wrong answer to a key question. What should you do?

options.text: Write the correct answer on the board and ask them to copy it
Move on because the syllabus is long and time is short
Find out why they made the mistake, reteach with a different example, then check again
Give extra homework using the same explanation as before

questions.explanation: A common error shows a misunderstanding; reteaching in a new way and re-checking addresses the cause.

questions.text: A pupil often squints, says the board is blurry and is falling behind. His marks were good last year. What is the best action?

options.text: Move him to the front, inform his parents and head teacher, and suggest an eye check
Ask a classmate to do his written work for him
Tell him he must try harder and concentrate like the other pupils if he wants good marks
Keep him at the back so he learns to be independent

questions.explanation: Possible sight problems should be supported at once and referred to parents and health services, not treated as laziness.

questions.text: A 12-year-old girl privately tells you that an adult at home beats her badly. She shows marks and asks you not to tell anyone. What should you do?

options.text: Promise secrecy and go to her home that same evening to confront the adult yourself directly
Listen calmly, do not promise secrecy, and report to the head teacher using school procedure
Wait a few weeks to see whether more marks appear on her before you decide to tell anyone at school
Ask other pupils in her class whether her story is true before you take any action at all about it

questions.explanation: A child at risk must be protected; teachers report through the proper channel and must not promise secrecy or investigate alone.

description: Checks ability to set routines, use positive discipline, manage large classes, keep learners engaged and treat every learner fairly.

competencies.name: Routines and classroom organisation
competencies.description: Sets and practises routines for starting, moving, handing out materials and ending lessons.

competencies.name: Positive behaviour and discipline
competencies.description: Uses clear rules, praise and calm responses to guide behaviour without harming learners.

competencies.name: Managing large classes
competencies.description: Organises seating, materials and group work in classes of 40 to 100 pupils.

competencies.name: Engagement and use of time
competencies.description: Gains attention and keeps lesson time productive.

competencies.name: Fairness and respect for learners
competencies.description: Treats all learners fairly and acts when a learner is treated harshly or unfairly.

questions.text: Why should a teacher teach and practise classroom routines in the first days of a term?

options.text: Pupils know what to do, so less time is lost and fewer problems start
Routines remove the need to prepare lessons carefully for the rest of the term
Routines keep pupils completely silent for the whole day
Routines show pupils early that the teacher is very strict

questions.explanation: Practised routines make expectations clear, save learning time and prevent many behaviour problems.

questions.text: Which is the best way to set classroom rules?

options.text: Let the head teacher announce rules without any explanation
Agree a few clear, positive rules with pupils and display them
Write a long list of rules with a clear punishment for each one that is broken
Make rules only after pupils have misbehaved

questions.explanation: Few, clear rules that pupils helped to make are easier to understand, remember and follow.

questions.text: Two pupils are chatting while you teach. Which response is best first?

options.text: Announce that they are the noisiest pupils in the class
Move closer or use a quiet signal, then give a short private reminder if needed
Send them out of the classroom for the rest of the lesson
Shout their names loudly so that the whole class hears and learns that talking is not allowed

questions.explanation: Low-key, private responses stop minor misbehaviour without embarrassing pupils or wasting lesson time.

questions.text: You have 80 pupils and only 20 textbooks. Which arrangement works best?

options.text: Give books to the best pupils and let the others watch
Pass the books around the class one pupil at a time until every pupil has had a turn
Groups of four with one book each and clear roles such as reader and recorder
Leave the books unused and only talk to the class

questions.explanation: Group work with defined roles lets many pupils use limited resources and stay active.

questions.text: Which is the most effective way to get a noisy class's attention?

options.text: Wait silently at the front without speaking or doing anything, even if it takes the whole lesson
Use a signal the class has practised, such as a raised hand or clap pattern
Shout louder than the pupils until they stop
Hit the table with a stick at the start of every lesson

questions.explanation: A practised signal is calm, quick and can be used again and again without raising your voice.

questions.text: Which strategies help manage a class of about 90 pupils? Select all that apply.

options.text: Group leaders who keep their group on task and report back
Avoiding questions to the back rows because they are far away
Clear routines and pupil helpers for giving out and collecting books
Teaching only by whole-class lecture so everyone hears the same thing
Seating in groups with a lane so you can walk through the room

questions.explanation: Routines, helpers, accessible seating and group leaders make a big class manageable and keep all pupils involved.

questions.text: Which feedback best reinforces good behaviour?

options.text: "Amina, thank you for raising your hand and waiting; it let everyone hear Juma."
"Sit down, you are always the noisy one."
"Good, class."
"Finally you are behaving like normal pupils."

questions.explanation: Specific praise tells the pupil exactly which behaviour was good, so it is more likely to be repeated.

questions.text: Two pupils begin pushing each other during a lesson. What should you do first?

options.text: Calmly separate them, then speak with each one later and follow school procedure
Join in by shouting at both pupils in front of the whole class until they stop
Ignore it so the pupils learn to settle it themselves without the teacher's help
Ask the other pupils to decide who is guilty and punish him in front of the class

questions.explanation: Safety comes first; a calm separation followed by private discussion addresses the cause and respects procedure.

questions.text: Your class comes back from break noisy and you lose ten minutes every day settling them. What is the best long-term solution?

options.text: Ask the head teacher to shorten the break
Shout at pupils until they sit down every time
Teach a re-entry routine: stand at the door, pupils enter quietly and begin a task on the board
Cancel the first ten minutes of each lesson after break

questions.explanation: A practised re-entry routine with a ready task turns lost time into learning time.

questions.text: You see a colleague hit a pupil hard in anger, leaving marks on the pupil's arm. What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing because the colleague is more senior than you and knows the pupils better
Discuss it with other pupils to see who agrees that the colleague was wrong to do it
Tell the pupil to behave better so that it does not happen again in any of the future lessons
Make sure the pupil gets care and report it to the head teacher using school procedure

questions.explanation: Harmful or humiliating punishment is not acceptable; staff must protect the pupil and report to the head teacher.

questions.text: One pupil disturbs your lessons every day, and reminders have not worked. What is the best next step?

options.text: Make him stand outside the classroom for the whole term so others can learn in peace
Send him to the head teacher at the start of every lesson until his behaviour changes
Meet him privately to find the cause, agree a plan, and involve parents if needed
Tell the whole class that he is the worst pupil in the school so that he feels ashamed

questions.explanation: Repeated misbehaviour usually has a cause; a private talk and agreed plan, with support, works better than exclusion or shaming.

questions.text: You notice that you usually ask the same few pupils at the front to answer questions. What should you do?

options.text: Ask only the pupils who raise their hands the fastest, since they are the most interested
Use a fair method such as a name list so every pupil gets a chance to answer
Continue, because those pupils always give correct answers
Stop asking questions so no one feels left out

questions.explanation: Giving all pupils a chance to take part is fair and shows every learner they matter.

description: Checks ability to prepare schemes of work and lesson plans, write measurable objectives, and use fair formative and summative assessment.

competencies.name: Schemes of work and lesson planning
competencies.description: Prepares schemes of work and lesson plans that fit the syllabus and the available time.

competencies.name: Learning objectives and competency-based design
competencies.description: Writes measurable objectives and aligns activities and assessment with them.

competencies.name: Formative assessment and feedback
competencies.description: Checks learning during lessons and gives useful feedback.

competencies.name: Test quality and fair marking
competencies.description: Designs valid tests and marks them honestly and fairly.

competencies.name: Using results to improve teaching
competencies.description: Analyses results to find weaknesses and improve teaching.

questions.competency: Schemes of work and lesson planning
questions.text: What is a scheme of work?

options.text: A detailed plan for teaching one lesson on one day
A timetable that shows when examinations will be held
A plan that divides the syllabus into topics across the weeks of a term or year
A record of every pupil's marks and attendance in each test and exercise of the term

questions.explanation: A scheme of work spreads syllabus content across the available weeks; a lesson plan covers a single lesson.

questions.text: Which verb is best for a measurable learning objective?

options.text: Calculate
Know about
Appreciate
Understand

questions.explanation: 'Calculate' describes something you can observe and check; the other verbs describe inner states that cannot be directly measured.

questions.competency: Schemes of work and lesson planning
questions.text: Which items should a good lesson plan include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teaching and learning activities for teacher and pupils
The names and occupations of pupils' parents
A way to check learning during or at the end of the lesson
Learning objectives for the lesson
The fee balances of the pupils in the class

questions.explanation: A lesson plan sets objectives, activities and a way of checking whether the objectives were achieved.

questions.text: Which is an example of formative assessment?

options.text: A short exit question at the end of a lesson that the teacher reads to see who understood
An admission test taken before joining the school
The annual class ranking printed on the report card
The end-of-year national examination that decides which pupils proceed to the next level of education

questions.explanation: Formative assessment is used during teaching to see understanding and adjust the next steps.

questions.text: Which feedback on a pupil's written work is most useful?

options.text: A short comment such as 'Poor work'
Specific comments on what is correct and one clear step to improve
A grade and the pupil's position in the class, compared with all other pupils
Only a tick or a cross on each question

questions.explanation: Useful feedback is specific and tells the learner how to improve, not only how well they did.

questions.text: When is a test considered valid?

options.text: When it measures the topics and skills that were taught and meant to be assessed
When it is long and has many questions
When it can be marked very quickly
When it is difficult enough that only a few of the very best pupils in the class can pass

questions.explanation: Validity means the test measures what it is supposed to measure, in line with the objectives and syllabus.

questions.text: What does competency-based assessment mainly require pupils to do?

options.text: Finish the whole syllabus faster than other pupils and other classes in the school
Take only written tests at the end of the term
Show that they can apply knowledge and skills in real tasks
Memorise facts and repeat them in the exam

questions.explanation: Competency-based assessment checks what learners can do with their knowledge and skills in realistic tasks.

questions.competency: Schemes of work and lesson planning
questions.text: Your scheme of work covers 12 weeks, but two weeks were lost to school events. What should you do?

options.text: Remove topics randomly without telling anyone in the department or the head teacher
Review the scheme, prioritise essential topics, and inform the head of department
Skip all assessments for the rest of the term so that you can teach every topic
Teach all topics as fast as possible without checking understanding along the way

questions.explanation: Planning should be adjusted openly, focusing on the most important learning and still checking understanding.

questions.text: After marking a test, you see that most pupils scored very low on questions about one topic. What is the best next step?

options.text: Remove those questions and give everyone full marks
Check whether the topic was taught well and the questions were clear, then reteach and review
Tell the pupils they did not study hard enough and ask them to revise the whole topic again at home
Record the marks and move on to the next topic

questions.explanation: Results show where teaching or testing may have problems; reteaching helps learners while also improving future tests.

questions.text: A colleague asks you to increase the marks of your weaker class so that the school average looks better. What should you do?

options.text: Agree, because the school's reputation is more important
Change the marks only for the pupils who are close to passing
Refuse to change the marks, and report the concern to the head of department if the pressure continues
Add a few marks to every pupil so no one is noticed

questions.explanation: Marks must honestly reflect pupils' performance; changing them is dishonest and hides learning problems.

questions.text: You must check 80 exercise books but cannot write detailed comments for every pupil. What is the best approach?

options.text: Give every pupil a tick without reading the work, so that all the books are returned by Friday
Stop marking exercise books for the term and use the time to prepare new lessons instead of marking
Mark only the books of the best pupils and leave the rest of the books until next term begins
Give whole-class feedback on common errors, use peer marking with a key, and sample-check

questions.explanation: Targeted and shared feedback methods make feedback manageable in big classes while still helping learning.

questions.text: Your objective is 'pupils will write a formal letter', but the plan only has you reading a sample letter, with no check at the end. What is the best improvement?

options.text: Add guided practice where pupils write a letter, and check it against a few clear criteria
Keep the plan and read a second sample letter
Change the objective to 'pupils will listen to a letter'
Keep the plan and give a dictation exercise for homework

questions.explanation: Activities and assessment should match the objective; pupils must practise and be checked on writing the letter.

description: Checks knowledge of pre-primary (awali) teaching: child development, play-based learning, early literacy and numeracy, safety and working with parents.

competencies.name: Child development
competencies.description: Understands how young children grow and learn, including emotional needs.

competencies.name: Play-based learning
competencies.description: Uses play and hands-on activities, and observation, rather than formal drilling.

competencies.name: Early literacy and numeracy
competencies.description: Builds early language, reading and number skills through age-appropriate activities.

competencies.name: Safety, health and protection
competencies.description: Keeps young children safe, healthy and protected from harm.

competencies.name: Working with parents
competencies.description: Communicates with parents about how young children learn.

questions.text: How do children aged 4 to 6 learn best in pre-primary school?

options.text: By sitting silently and memorising lessons
Through play, songs, stories and hands-on activities
By copying long notes from the board each day and reading them aloud together
By taking written tests every week

questions.explanation: Young children learn through active play, talking and handling real objects.

questions.text: What should a teacher do while young children play outside?

options.text: Ask older pupils from Standard Six to supervise them without any adult present
Supervise them all the time and check that the area is free from hazards
Allow them to play alone while she marks books inside
Lock them in the classroom so that no one gets hurt

questions.explanation: Young children need constant adult supervision, and the play area must be safe.

questions.text: In a pre-primary class, some children speak in full sentences while others use only a few words. How should the teacher think about this?

options.text: Children develop at different rates, so she should support each child without comparing them
The slower children are lazy and need to be punished
All children should reach the same level by the end of the first month of school, whatever their age or home background
Slower children should be moved to another class immediately

questions.explanation: Children grow at different rates; teachers provide support and monitor progress without labelling.

questions.text: Which activity best builds early reading skills?

options.text: Reading aloud alone in front of the class
Copying long sentences from the board
Writing each letter 50 times in a notebook every morning before play
Songs, rhymes, stories and talking about pictures

questions.explanation: Listening to and enjoying language builds vocabulary and sound awareness, which prepare children for reading.

questions.text: Which activities build early number skills? Select all that apply.

options.text: Counting stones, bottle tops or seeds
Sorting objects by size and colour
Writing the multiplication table 20 times
Copying long addition sums from a textbook
Singing counting songs with actions

questions.explanation: Handling real objects and singing build number sense; written drill is too advanced for this age.

questions.text: A new pre-primary child speaks only her mother tongue at home. What is the best approach?

options.text: Welcome her home language and slowly build Kiswahili with songs and objects
Ignore her until she begins speaking Kiswahili like the other children in class
Punish her whenever she speaks her mother tongue so that she learns Kiswahili faster
Teach her in English only, since English will be the main language she needs later

questions.explanation: Respecting the home language and building the school language through meaningful activity helps children feel safe and learn.

questions.text: What is the best way to check the progress of a pre-primary child?

options.text: Ask each child to recite the whole alphabet alone
Give a written exam at the end of each term and record every child's total marks
Rank the children by position in the class
Observe the child during play and keep simple records or samples of work

questions.explanation: Observation during natural activities shows what young children can really do.

questions.text: A 4-year-old cries every morning when her mother leaves. What should the teacher do?

options.text: Scold her for crying in front of the other children so that she stops crying quickly
Let the parent stay in the room all day until the child stops crying completely
Ask the parent to leave quietly without saying goodbye so the child does not notice
Greet her warmly, allow a short goodbye, then comfort her and offer an activity

questions.explanation: A warm, predictable goodbye and comforting activity help the child feel secure.

questions.text: A child has a fever and keeps vomiting at school. What should the teacher do?

options.text: Keep the child comfortable and supervised, tell the head teacher and contact the parent or guardian
Ask the child to rest and continue the lesson as normal
Send the child home alone on foot
Give the child medicine from her own bag

questions.explanation: A sick young child needs adult care and prompt contact with the family; teachers should not give medicine.

questions.text: A 5-year-old girl tells you that an older man who collects her sometimes touches her private parts. What should you do?

options.text: Wait for a week to see if it happens again, then tell her parents at the next meeting
Ask her to show you exactly what he did, using a doll or a drawing, to be sure
Confront the man when he comes to collect her and warn him in front of other parents
Listen calmly, do not promise secrecy, and report at once to the head teacher

questions.explanation: The child must be protected quickly through the proper channel, without repeated questioning or promises of secrecy.

questions.text: The head teacher asks you to make your 5-year-olds sit and copy long text to prepare for Standard One. What is the best response?

options.text: Stop all writing activities for the whole year
Explain respectfully why play-based activities suit their age and suggest short pre-writing activities
Ignore the request and say nothing
Follow the instruction completely, since you cannot disagree

questions.explanation: Teachers can respectfully advise on age-appropriate practice, such as pre-writing play, while cooperating with the school.

questions.text: A parent says: 'My child only plays at school and does not write. Why am I paying fees?' What is the best response?

options.text: Tell the parent that the school's methods are not open to question or discussion
Tell the parent to hire a private tutor for writing lessons after school each day
Say that the child is behind and must start long writing tasks from next week
Explain that play builds reading and writing skills, and show her child's work

questions.explanation: Parents accept play-based learning more when teachers explain its purpose and show evidence of progress.

description: Checks ability to identify learners with disabilities or learning difficulties, teach inclusively, plan individual support and work respectfully with families and specialists.

competencies.name: Identifying learners' needs
competencies.description: Notices signs of disability or learning difficulty and responds carefully.

competencies.name: Inclusive teaching strategies
competencies.description: Adapts teaching, seating and materials so all learners can take part.

competencies.name: Individual plans and supports
competencies.description: Understands and uses individual education plans and realistic goals.

competencies.name: Attitudes, rights and respect
competencies.description: Uses respectful language and challenges stigma and teasing.

competencies.name: Working with parents and specialists
competencies.description: Works with parents, school leaders and health or special education services.

questions.text: Which phrase shows respectful language about a learner?

options.text: "The abnormal pupil"
"The handicapped child in my class"
"A learner with a disability"
"One of the slow ones"

questions.explanation: Person-first language puts the learner before the disability and avoids labels.

questions.text: Which sign might suggest that a learner has a hearing difficulty?

options.text: Prefers to play football at break time
Often asks others to repeat, and does not respond when called from behind
Writes neatly and finishes written work quickly, before most of the other learners
Is quiet during group discussions

questions.explanation: Repeated requests to repeat and not reacting to sounds from behind may show hearing difficulty and need follow-up.

questions.text: How should you support a learner with low vision, including some learners with albinism?

options.text: Write in small letters to save chalk and fit more notes on the board
Always let a classmate copy the notes instead of expecting the learner to read
Seat the learner near the front and write large and clear on the board
Seat the learner at the back of the class so the others can see the board

questions.explanation: Front seating, large clear writing and good contrast help learners with low vision to see and take part.

questions.text: What is an individual education plan (IEP)?

options.text: A plan for waiving a learner's school fees
A list of all learners who have a disability, kept by the head teacher for the school inspectors
A written plan with goals, support and review dates for one learner
A disciplinary record for learners who misbehave

questions.explanation: An IEP sets personal goals and supports for a learner and is reviewed regularly.

questions.text: Which supports help a learner who has serious difficulty with reading? Select all that apply.

options.text: Giving extra time and short, clear instructions
Using pictures and reading aloud together
Asking the learner to read alone in front of the class daily
Teaching in small steps with repeated practice
Reducing marks for every spelling mistake in all subjects

questions.explanation: Extra time, multi-sensory support and small steps help; public reading and penalties for spelling often discourage the learner.

questions.text: Before deciding that a learner has a learning disability, what should a teacher do?

options.text: Decide quickly from one poor test result, then place the learner in a special school at once
Observe over time in different activities, keep notes, and consult parents and specialists
Label the learner as lazy so he works harder
Ask other pupils whether the learner is slow

questions.explanation: A careful, shared assessment is needed; teachers observe and refer, and do not diagnose alone.

questions.text: Which approach is most inclusive in a class that includes learners with disabilities?

options.text: Plan lessons with several ways for learners to access content, take part and show what they know
Teach learners with disabilities in a separate room at all times
Exempt learners with disabilities from all assessments
Teach all learners in the same way, at the same speed, and expect the same output from every learner in the class

questions.explanation: Inclusive planning offers different routes to learning and ways of showing learning, so all learners can take part.

questions.text: Pupils laugh when a boy who stammers reads aloud. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore it because children always tease one another, and he must learn to accept it as part of school
Make him read aloud more often until he is cured
Excuse him from all speaking in class
Stop the teasing calmly, teach respect, and give the boy time and choices about how to take part

questions.explanation: Teachers must stop teasing and create a safe environment while supporting the learner's participation.

questions.text: A learner who uses crutches cannot easily reach your classroom, which is up several steps. What is the best action?

options.text: Ask the head teacher for changes, such as a ground-floor room or a ramp
Teach him separately at home until the school can find a suitable classroom for him
Ask his parents to carry him up the steps every day before the lessons begin
Allow him to skip every lesson that is held in a classroom upstairs

questions.explanation: Schools should remove barriers so the learner can participate fully and safely.

questions.text: A learner with an intellectual disability cannot do the Standard Five mathematics tasks. What is the best approach?

options.text: Let him draw during mathematics lessons
Give him the lowest marks and move on
Set smaller, achievable goals on the same topic in his IEP, give extra support, and review progress
Give him the same tasks as everyone else with no help

questions.explanation: Realistic, individual goals with support allow the learner to make progress and stay part of the class.

questions.text: A mother of a child with albinism wants to keep her at home because she fears for her safety and teasing at school. What is the best response?

options.text: Tell her that her fears are only superstition and that nothing will happen to her child
Agree that the child should stay at home until she is older and the teasing has stopped
Listen with empathy, explain the school's safety measures, and plan safe travel
Warn her that the child will be removed from the register if she does not attend

questions.explanation: Respectful listening and joint safety planning keep the child in school and protect her.

questions.text: A learner repeatedly fails to copy notes and seems not to hear instructions. What should you do?

options.text: Suspend the learner until the behaviour improves
Wait until the next school level to see if things improve
Move the learner to the back of the class
Tell the head teacher and parents, and ask for a health or special education assessment

questions.explanation: Persistent difficulties should be reported to the school and family and referred for proper assessment.

description: Checks counselling basics, confidentiality and its limits, referral, handling bullying and abuse disclosures, and career guidance for learners.

competencies.name: Counselling basics and listening
competencies.description: Listens actively and responds with empathy to learners in distress.

competencies.name: Confidentiality and ethics
competencies.description: Protects learners' private information and explains the limits of confidentiality.

competencies.name: Referral and working with others
competencies.description: Knows when to refer and who to involve for learner safety and wellbeing.

competencies.name: Bullying and abuse disclosures
competencies.description: Responds correctly when a learner reports bullying or abuse.

competencies.name: Career and academic guidance
competencies.description: Helps learners explore realistic study and career options.

questions.text: Which describes active listening?

options.text: Giving full attention, reflecting what the learner says, and asking open questions
Telling your own similar story to show you understand
Writing notes while looking away from the learner
Interrupting quickly to give the learner advice, because you have more experience than she does

questions.explanation: Active listening means focusing on the learner and showing that you understand.

questions.text: What does confidentiality mean in school counselling?

options.text: Everything a learner says is always kept secret from everyone
What the learner says is always reported to the parents
What a learner shares is kept private, except when someone's safety is at risk
What the learner says is shared with all the teachers, so they can support the learner in class

questions.explanation: Counsellors protect privacy but must act when there is serious risk of harm.

questions.text: Which response shows empathy to a learner who says 'I feel alone since my mother travelled'?

options.text: "Don't worry about it; many children feel like this and it will soon pass, so go back to class."
"It sounds like you have been feeling very alone since your mother went away."
"Other children have worse problems than you."
"You should be stronger than this."

questions.explanation: Empathy reflects the learner's feelings without judging or minimising them.

questions.text: When should a school counsellor refer a learner to another professional?

options.text: Never, because counsellors should deal with every problem alone
Only when the learner's parent asks for it
For every problem, immediately, without first listening
When the problem is beyond the counsellor's role, such as serious mental health, medical need or abuse

questions.explanation: Referral protects learners when needs go beyond school counselling.

questions.text: Which is good career guidance for a Form Four student?

options.text: Help him explore his interests, results and options, including vocational training
Tell the student which career to choose because you know the job market better
Encourage everyone to choose only medicine or engineering because they pay the most
Choose the career that the parents prefer, since they are paying for the studies

questions.explanation: Career guidance gives information and helps the learner make an informed choice.

questions.text: In which situations must a counsellor break confidentiality and act? Select all that apply.

options.text: A learner says he dislikes a teacher's lessons
A learner says he failed a test and feels sad
A learner reports that an adult is sexually abusing her
A learner threatens to seriously hurt another person
A learner says she plans to harm herself

questions.explanation: Confidentiality has limits when there is serious risk of harm to the learner or others.

questions.text: Where should a counsellor keep notes from counselling sessions?

options.text: In a locked place that only the counsellor can access
On the notice board for the learner to review
In the learner's general class file
In an open file in the staff room where all teachers can read it when needed

questions.explanation: Counselling records are sensitive and should be kept secure and private.

questions.text: A Form Two girl says she has felt hopeless and not slept for weeks. What is the best response?

options.text: Tell the class what she said so that her friends can cheer her up and keep her company
Ask her to pray and come back to see you next term if she still feels the same way
Tell her to be strong and keep it to herself because others have worse problems
Listen, ask about thoughts of self-harm, and involve the guardian and a clinician

questions.explanation: Signs of serious distress need careful asking about safety, involvement of responsible adults and professional referral.

questions.text: A boy tells you that older boys bully him in the dormitory and begs you not to tell anyone. What should you do?

options.text: Confront the older boys publicly in the dining hall so that everyone sees the bullying stop
Advise him to fight back so that the older boys stop bothering him in the dormitory
Support him, explain that you must act to keep him safe, and report to the head teacher
Promise secrecy and do nothing else, since he trusts only you with what he told you

questions.explanation: Bullying must be addressed for the learner's safety; be honest with him about the steps and report properly.

questions.text: A 14-year-old girl tells you that her uncle touches her at night. What should you do?

options.text: Tell her to avoid her uncle and take no further action, as it is a family matter
Question the uncle yourself to learn the truth before telling anyone else at school
Counsel her for several weeks before telling anyone, so that she is not frightened
Listen and reassure her, then report at once to the head teacher

questions.explanation: Abuse disclosures must be reported at once through the proper channel; counsellors do not investigate themselves.

questions.text: A Form Four student with low marks wants a course that needs very high marks, and his family is pressuring him. What is the best guidance?

options.text: Discuss realistic options, including vocational training or retaking subjects, and respect his final decision
Promise him he will succeed if he wants it enough
Choose a course for him that you think is best
Tell him to give up his dream completely

questions.explanation: Honest information about realistic routes helps the learner make a good decision.

questions.text: A student starts to cry in your office and cannot speak. What should you do?

options.text: Send her back to class until she can talk
Call her classmates to comfort her
Demand that she explains right now, because you have other learners waiting to see you
Stay calm and patient, give her time, and tell her you are there when she is ready

questions.explanation: Calm patience gives the learner safety and time to start talking.
